items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I didn’t see Jimmie Noone, because he left around 1917, 1918, ’19, ’20

ctx.x: You mentioned a lot of legendary people in the brass band: Manny Perez. Black Benny, who Louis Armstrong talks about. Jelly Roll [Morton] talks about him. Who were some of the people you saw that had eventually come to have big names, because I imagine you saw a lot of these people before they left New Orleans for good, before the late teens.

Red Allen. Guy Kelly. I didn’t see Jimmie Noone, because he left around 1917, 1918, ’19, ’20, and I wasn’t old enough to realize what I was looking at, knew who these people were. But I knew of them, that they went away. I heard of the Baquet family. I heard of Sidney Bechet. He was a legend. He went when he was around 16 years old. He started traveling with carnival shows and minstrel shows. He was such a phenomenon at that time. People had never heard nobody blow a horn like that. He was a frustrated trumpet…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: we went there to meet him

ctx.x: Yeah, Jimmie Noone was a great clarinet player.

Yeah. And he came to New York and he organized a band and went into the Savoy, we went there to meet him, and he went there -- and it lasted around two weeks, and he went back to Chicago. That's around 1932, 1931... [June 1932] Things were slowing down in Chicago, so he came on through. And he had Vincent/Richard(?) (?) in his band.
Piano player. He was a great piano player.

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: And all the real wildcats at the left, like Jim and Noom, John of Dodge, Bonnie de Gat was around

ctx.x: Willie Humphrey, the one that's working with Paul now. Earl Humphrey's brother. He impressed me, but he lived uptown and never had a chance much to him. And he's the one that impressed me, I thought he was a master. There were others, like Big Al Lloyd, who was always in the same track in the summer of retirement. He played if he got a chance. I worked with him, I know him at Twy, and Walter DeCoult, four of us at the Bungalow. Out on the Shellback Road, I worked a couple of months out there with them. He was…
